body:
Tamil devotional hymns

Among the earliest major regional Bhakti traditions were those of the Tamil-speaking Alvars and Nayanars. These saint-poets travelled to sacred places and composed hymns in praise of their chosen deities. Their songs subsequently became part of temple worship and religious literature.

FeatureAlvarsNayanars
Number traditionally recognized1263
Principal deityVishnuShiva
LanguageTamilTamil
Important compositionsNalayira Divya PrabandhamTevaram and associated Shaiva hymn literature

The Nalayira Divya Prabandham is the collection of approximately 4000 sacred compositions attributed to the Alvars. It is sometimes called the Tamil Veda. Andal, a woman saint, is one of the celebrated Alvars.

The Tevaram contains hymns composed by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar. The Tiruvacakam of Manikkavasagar is another major work of Tamil Shaiva devotional literature.

Under Chola patronage, the singing of Shaiva hymns became an established part of temple worship. This illustrates how an orally performed tradition can become preserved within religious institutions and written collections.

Maharashtra: Abhang and the Varkari tradition

An abhang is a Marathi devotional poetic composition particularly associated with the Varkari tradition. The term conveys the idea of something unbroken.

The Varkari tradition centres on devotion to Vitthala, also known as Vithoba or Panduranga, at Pandharpur in Maharashtra. Vitthala is worshipped as a form of Vishnu or Krishna.

Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram and Chokhamela are important saint-poets associated with the Marathi Bhakti tradition. Tukaram is especially renowned for his abhangs.

The annual pilgrimage to Pandharpur, known as the Wari, provides an important setting for collective devotional singing. Abhangs communicate faith, humility, compassion and service to others.

North Indian devotional compositions

Saint-poetPrincipal associationImportant composition or collection
KabirNirguna devotionSakhis and pads; Bijak
TulsidasRama devotionRamcharitmanas in Awadhi
SurdasKrishna devotionSursagar
MirabaiKrishna devotionDevotional bhajans

Kabir's verses were preserved through wandering singers and later collections. Compositions attributed to him appear in the Bijak, Panch Vani and Guru Granth Sahib. His tradition demonstrates the relationship between oral poetry, devotional singing and written preservation.

Jayadeva and Krishna devotional literature

Jayadeva composed the Gita Govinda in Sanskrit in the 12th century. The work portrays the love of Radha and Krishna as an expression of divine devotion.

The Gita Govinda contains lyrical compositions commonly known as Ashtapadis, associated with sets of 8 verses. Its songs have an important place in Indian devotional music and dance traditions, including the worship traditions associated with the Jagannath Temple at Puri.

Assam: Borgeet and Shankaradeva

Srimanta Shankaradeva was a major Vaishnava saint and cultural figure of Assam. His religious tradition is known as Eka Sarana Nama Dharma, emphasizing surrender to the one Supreme Being through devotion.

Shankaradeva and his disciple Madhavadeva are associated with Borgeet, the Assamese Vaishnava tradition of devotional songs. These compositions are distinguished from the festive folk songs known as Bihu Geet.

  • Kirtana-ghosha: An important devotional composition of Shankaradeva.
  • Namghar: A community prayer and devotional gathering hall.
  • Satra: A Vaishnava religious institution serving spiritual, educational and cultural purposes.

Manipur: Sankirtana

Manipuri Sankirtana is a Vaishnava ritual tradition combining singing, drumming and dancing. Its narratives principally concern Krishna. It accompanies religious festivals and important ceremonies in the lives of members of the community.

UNESCO inscribed Sankirtana, ritual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipur on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013.

Prelims focus

  • 12 Alvars: Vishnu; 63 Nayanars: Shiva.
  • Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar are associated with the Tevaram.
  • Abhang is associated with Marathi Bhakti, Tukaram and Pandharpur.
  • Jayadeva composed the Sanskrit Gita Govinda.
  • Shankaradeva is associated with Kirtana-ghosha, Namghar and Satra traditions.
  • Trap: Manipuri Sankirtana includes singing, drumming and dancing, not merely the recitation of religious verses.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 8, pp. 105–109, 113–117; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, pp. 143–146; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, devotional and performing arts traditions; The Sentinel, Borgeet: Through the Centuries, 19 July 2026; UNESCO, Sankirtana of Manipur, nomination file 00843, Decision 8.COM 8.14; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Major Devotional Music Traditions, Saints and Sacred Compositions

body:
Qawwali and the Sufi tradition

Qawwali is a South Asian Sufi devotional musical tradition that expresses spiritual longing, divine love, praise and remembrance of God. It is particularly associated with the Chishti Sufi order.

Sufi traditions emphasize inner spiritual realization and devotion. Music and poetry became important means of communicating spiritual ideas among Sufi teachers, disciples and wider communities.

Sama, zikr and qawwali

  • Sama: Devotional listening, particularly listening to mystical music or spiritual poetry.
  • Zikr: Remembrance of God through the repetition of divine names or sacred formulas.
  • Qawwali: A musical tradition that may form part of Sufi devotional gatherings and sama.
  • Qawwal: A performer of qawwali.

Sama is a broader spiritual practice than any single musical genre. Similarly, zikr is not necessarily a musical performance.

Important Sufi associations

Amir Khusrau, a poet, musician and disciple of the Chishti saint Nizamuddin Auliya, is closely associated with the historical development of Indo-Islamic musical and poetic traditions, including qawwali. It is more accurate to recognize his major traditional association with qawwali than to claim that he was its sole inventor.

Important Chishti centres include the dargah of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer and the dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi.

TermMeaning
KhanqahSufi hospice or spiritual gathering centre
DargahShrine associated with the tomb of a Sufi saint
ZiyaratVisit or pilgrimage to a sacred shrine

Qawwali performances at Sufi centres have historically attracted devotees and listeners from diverse social and religious backgrounds.

Shabad Kirtan in Sikhism

Shabad Kirtan refers to the devotional singing of sacred hymns in the Sikh tradition, especially hymns contained in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Guru Nanak established a practice of congregational worship through hymn singing at Kartarpur. The singing of sacred compositions became an important part of Sikh religious life.

Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604. The scripture includes compositions of Sikh Gurus as well as devotional poets such as Kabir and Namdev. The Guru Granth Sahib thus preserves contributions from a wider devotional heritage.

Shabad Kirtan is particularly associated with worship in the gurdwara. Its defining feature is the singing of sacred hymns rather than the use of any particular instrument.

Ginan tradition

Ginans are devotional compositions associated particularly with the Khoja Ismaili Muslim tradition. The word is related to the Sanskrit term jnana, meaning knowledge.

Ginans communicate spiritual and religious ideas through regional languages, including Gujarati, Kachchhi, Sindhi, Punjabi and Hindi. They have been sung in prayer gatherings and passed orally from one generation to another.

Some ginans were subsequently recorded in the Khojaki script. This tradition illustrates the interaction between religious teachings, local languages and oral musical transmission in western India, including Gujarat.

Harikatha and religious storytelling

Harikatha is a devotional storytelling tradition that combines narration, religious explanation and music. It communicates stories associated with sacred literature and religious figures to assembled audiences.

Harikatha is especially prominent in parts of southern India. Its narrative character distinguishes it from the singing of an individual devotional lyric, although both may belong to the broader tradition of Bhakti.

Comparison by devotional purpose

TraditionReligious associationCharacteristic feature
BhajanEspecially Hindu Bhakti traditionsDevotional song or spiritual instruction
QawwaliSufi IslamMystical musical expression
Shabad KirtanSikhismSinging of sacred hymns
GinanIsmaili traditionRegional-language devotional knowledge
HarikathaHindu devotional traditionsReligious storytelling with music

Prelims focus

  • Qawwali is particularly associated with the Chishti Sufi tradition.
  • Amir Khusrau was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.
  • Shabad Kirtan belongs to Sikh devotional worship.
  • Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604.
  • Ginans are associated with the Khoja Ismaili tradition and include Gujarati and Kachchhi compositions.
  • Trap: Sama is devotional listening and is broader than qawwali alone.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 8, pp. 110–119; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, pp. 151, 155–157; IGNOU, Basic Principles and Techniques of Communication, section Folk Oral Literature and Folk Music, consulted 26 November 2026.]
title: Qawwali, Shabad Kirtan and Other Devotional Singing Traditions

body:
Development of devotional singing in Gujarat

Gujarat possesses a rich tradition of devotional poetry expressed through bhajans, padas, prabhatiyas, garbis and other regional compositions. Vaishnava Bhakti, the worship of the goddess and the teachings of regional saints have all contributed to this tradition.

The use of Gujarati and related regional languages enabled devotional teachings to reach ordinary households and village communities. Many compositions entered oral tradition and became familiar even among people who could not read the original written texts.

Narsinh Mehta

Narsinh Mehta, also known as Narsi Mehta, was a prominent 15th-century Gujarati saint-poet associated with Talaja and Junagadh in Saurashtra. He is traditionally celebrated as Adikavi, or the pioneering poet of Gujarati literature.

His poetry centres particularly on devotion to Krishna. It combines religious love with human compassion, humility and concern for people suffering from social exclusion.

Important musical and literary associations

  • Vaishnav Jan To: A famous devotional composition expressing compassion, humility and ethical conduct as qualities of a true devotee. It later became closely associated with Mahatma Gandhi.
  • Prabhatiya: A morning devotional song. Narsinh Mehta's Prabhatiyas form an important part of Gujarat's devotional heritage.
  • Pada: A lyrical poetic composition frequently intended for singing, often expressing devotional emotion or spiritual experience.
  • Sudamacharitra: A composition associated with Narsinh Mehta that narrates the story of Krishna and Sudama.

The ethical significance of Vaishnav Jan To lies in its connection between devotion and sensitivity to the suffering of other human beings. It demonstrates that devotional music may communicate social and moral values as well as praise of a deity.

Mirabai

Mirabai was a 16th-century Rajput saint-poet associated with Mewar in Rajasthan. Her devotional compositions express intense love for Krishna, whom she frequently addresses as Giridhar Gopal.

Although her principal historical association is with Rajasthan, her songs became widely popular in Gujarat. Traditional accounts also connect her later life with Dwarka.

Mirabai's compositions illustrate how a saint-poet's musical influence may extend beyond their original region through pilgrimage, wandering singers and oral transmission.

Dayaram

Dayaram was a major Gujarati Vaishnava poet who lived during the late 18th and early 19th centuries. He is particularly associated with the garbi as a devotional literary and musical form.

His garbis frequently express love for Krishna and the emotional world of Radha and the gopis. Dayaram helped establish the garbi as an important form of Gujarati devotional poetry.

Garbi compositions and Garba songs share historical and cultural connections, but the terms are not interchangeable in every literary or religious context.

Gangasati and Panbai

Gangasati was a woman saint associated with the devotional tradition of Saurashtra. Her bhajans are remembered particularly for their spiritual instruction.

A traditional collection of 52 bhajans attributed to Gangasati is understood as a series of teachings addressed to Panbai. These compositions explain spiritual discipline, devotion, the importance of the spiritual teacher and inner realization through accessible language.

The Gangasati tradition is an important example of the contribution of women to Gujarati devotional literature and oral musical heritage.

Haveli Sangeet and Pushtimarg

Haveli Sangeet is the devotional musical tradition associated with Pushtimarg, the Krishna-centred Vaishnava tradition founded by Vallabhacharya.

In this tradition, devotional compositions form part of the daily religious service, known as seva, offered to Krishna. Music accompanies different occasions of worship within the temple.

Vallabhacharya's son Vitthalnath organized the tradition of the Ashtachhap, a group of 8 poet-devotees whose compositions became particularly important in Krishna worship. Surdas, Kumbhandas and Nanddas were among the poets associated with this group.

Shrinathji's temple at Nathdwara in Rajasthan is an important centre of Pushtimarg devotional worship. Gujarat also has a substantial Haveli Sangeet tradition, including Vaishnava havelis in Ahmedabad.

Haveli Sangeet is principally a temple-based devotional music tradition. Its devotional compositions may draw upon established classical musical conventions; it should not be classified exclusively as rural folk music.

Prelims focus

  • Narsinh Mehta: Vaishnav Jan To and Prabhatiyas.
  • Mirabai: Krishna devotion, Mewar and popularity in Gujarat.
  • Dayaram: Gujarati devotional garbis.
  • Gangasati: bhajans traditionally addressed to Panbai.
  • Vallabhacharya: Pushtimarg; Vitthalnath: Ashtachhap tradition.
  • Trap: Nathdwara is located in Rajasthan, although Pushtimarg has a strong presence in Gujarat.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 7, English edition, 2021–22, Chapters 7–8, pp. 36–41; Social Science, Standard 10, English edition, Chapter 2, pp. 15–16; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 8, pp. 109, 114–115; Bharat Sangraha, Folk Songs of Saurashtra; Ahmedabad University, A Glimpse into Pushtimargiya Sangeet; The Indian Express, Rediscovering Haveli Sangeet, 2024; standalone Gujarat textbooks consulted in place of the unreadable project Volume 09; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
